dedupe_keys.name: copenhagen cloudburst management plan economics of blue green stormwater management

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes how the City of Copenhagen prepared its Cloudburst Management Plan in 2012, an offshoot of the Copenhagen Climate Adaptation Plan, after four major rainfall events in six years, the largest in 2011 causing more than DKK 6 billion of damage. The MIKE URBAN runoff model was used to map flood depths for 2010, 2060 and 2110 and for 10, 20 and 100-year events with and without adaptation, and a socio-economic assessment compared a traditional sewer solution (about DKK 20 billion) with a combined blue-green solution of cloudburst roads with high kerbs, new canals, lakes and green spaces plus pipes to the harbour (about DKK 13 billion); both cut damages by DKK 16 billion over 100 years, but only the combined solution gave a net gain, of about DKK 3 billion. The plan was detailed in 2013-2014 for seven catchments and broken into some 300 projects, about 15 a year over 20 to 30 years, coordinated with HOFOR, Frederiksberg and neighbouring utilities. The page is accessible online as free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal and was created in 2016. Caveats: figures are the city's own estimates, legal obstacles to using roads as flood ways are noted, and later progress is not reported. It illustrates investment appraisal and climate adaptation planning of green and blue infrastructure against pluvial flooding and relates to stormwater models such as MIKE URBAN and to land use data such as the Copernicus Urban Atlas.
name: Copenhagen Cloudburst Management Plan (economics of blue-green stormwater management)
outcomes: The combined blue-green and pipe solution was estimated at DKK 13 billion against DKK 20 billion for sewers alone, with the same DKK 16 billion damage reduction and a net socio-economic gain; 300 projects were scheduled over 20 to 30 years.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study contributed by the City of Copenhagen
resources_used: Danish Meteorological Institute precipitation projections (IPCC A2)
